notes.meaning: Balaam woke up early, saddled his donkey, and set out with the Moabite leaders. In those days, important people often rode donkeys, using a folded cloth or pad as a saddle. His quick start showed how eager he was to earn Balak's promised wealth.

God became angry because Balaam set out with a greedy heart, hoping for a way to curse Israel and gain riches. The angel of the Lord blocked the road like an enemy to stop his sinful course. Balaam was traveling with his two personal servants while his heart chased after money.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some critics think verse 22 clashes with God's permission in verse 20. They suggest the donkey story was added to the account later. Others answer that God was angry at Balaam's greedy heart on the way, not at the trip itself.

notes.meaning: The donkey saw the angel standing in the road holding an open sword, so she turned aside into an open field. Balaam was blind to the spiritual danger and could not see the angel at all. Furious that his ride went off course, he struck the animal to force her back onto the path.

The angel moved farther up the path and stood in a narrow walkway between two vineyards. These farm paths were pressed tight between stone and mud fences built to protect the grapes. There was very little room for anyone to get by safely.

Seeing the armed angel a second time, the donkey squeezed against the stone wall to squeeze past. This crushed Balaam's foot against the rocks. In his frustration and pain, Balaam beat the animal once again.

The angel moved farther ahead into an even tighter spot where the path had no room to turn right or left. God was closing in on Balaam, giving him nowhere to run. When people ignore early warnings, God often brings them into tighter corners.

When the donkey saw the angel blocking the narrow path with nowhere to go, she simply lay down on the ground. Balaam completely lost his temper and struck her hard with his wooden walking stick. He was blinded by rage while his animal was trying to protect him.

God performed a miracle and gave the donkey human speech. The animal asked Balaam why he had beaten her three times when she had done nothing wrong. God used a humble beast to correct a famous seer who thought he saw everything.

differ.view: Some who fully accept the miracle say we cannot know exactly how it happened. God may have given the donkey human words, or He may have turned her cries into words that only Balaam understood.

notes.meaning: Balaam was so wild with anger that he answered the donkey without even noticing how strange a talking animal was. He yelled that she had embarrassed him and made him look foolish. He even wished for a sword so he could kill her on the spot.

The donkey reminded Balaam that she had been his faithful mount for many years. She asked if she had ever acted like this before, and Balaam had to admit that she had not. Even an animal's past loyalty should have made him pause and rethink his anger.

The Lord removed the blind spots from Balaam's eyes so he could finally see the angel standing in the path with a drawn sword. Realizing the deadly danger he was in, Balaam instantly bowed low and fell flat on his face. Until God opens our eyes, we cannot see his judgment or his mercy.

The angel challenged Balaam for cruelly beating his innocent donkey three times. He declared that he had come out to block him because Balaam's journey was headstrong and driven by evil motives. God cares about how people treat animals and hates dishonest greed.

The angel told Balaam that the donkey had actually saved his life by turning away three times. If she had tried to push past, the angel would have killed Balaam and spared the beast. What looked like stubbornness in the animal was really God's mercy saving the man from death.

Balaam confessed that he had sinned, admitting he did not know the angel was standing in the road against him. He offered to turn back home if his journey displeased the Lord. Even so, his words sounded halfhearted, because his heart still secretly wanted Balak's riches.

The angel told Balaam to go on with Balak's messengers, but strictly commanded him to speak only the words God gave him. God permitted him to continue, but bound him under absolute control. Balaam would not be allowed to say whatever he wanted for profit.

When Balak heard that Balaam was arriving, he traveled out to the border city along the Arnon River to meet him. Meeting an honored guest at the far edge of the kingdom was an ancient way to show the deepest respect. Balak wanted to flatter Balaam so the seer would do his bidding.

Balak asked Balaam why he had refused the first urgent invitation to come. The king asked if Balaam doubted his power to give him great honor and rich rewards. Balak assumed that every man has a price that wealth can buy.

Balaam replied that although he had arrived, he had no power of his own to say whatever he liked. He warned the king that he was bound to speak only the exact message God put into his mouth. The experience with the donkey had shown Balaam that God was in complete command.

Balaam went with Balak to the city named Kiriath-huzoth. The king brought him into this bustling town to receive royal hospitality and begin their plans. This was their first stop before setting out to view the Israelite camp.

Balak slaughtered cattle and sheep for a grand feast to celebrate Balaam's arrival and seek the favor of his gods. He sent portions of the meat to Balaam and the princes who accompanied him. By eating food offered to pagan idols, Balaam showed how willing he was to compromise with false worship.

The next morning Balak led Balaam up to Bamoth-baal, a high place where the false god Baal was worshipped. From this hill, Balaam could look out and see the outer edge of Israel's vast camp. Balak believed the seer had to see the people with his own eyes for his magical curse to take effect.
